title: Introduction — Cultural & Acultural
paragraphs: Gershon opens with her own failure. Writing grant proposals for NOSA (the National Office of Samoan Affairs) in California, she kept "getting it all wrong": her arguments for supporting Samoan culture fell flat with US funders. The more experienced grant writers rewrote her sentences, and the lesson they had learned over forty years was blunt — when you present an ethnic group to US government funders, talk about race and class, not culture.

To see how that lesson was learned, she reads twenty-two old proposals from a now-defunct organization, Samoa mo Samoa, written between 1979 and 1995. Early proposals that described Samoans as a culture, or as migrants needing to assimilate, were rejected again and again. Only when writers reframed Samoans as an at-risk minority — citing poverty and the lowest test scores of any San Francisco minority — did the money come. In the US, Samoan organizations are fundable not because migrants might lose their culture but because they are "at risk," like other minorities.

This sets up the book's master pair of terms. The cultural is what people frame as traditional and locatable — authentic, tied to Samoa. The acultural is what they frame as modern and universal — bureaucracies, laws, capitalism, technology. Crucially, this is a folk classification, not an anthropological one: for an anthropologist all social life is cultural and nothing is acultural. Gershon studies how her interlocutors build and use this divide, and how, as she puts it, "the acultural haunts the cultural."

What a government counts as culture, she argues, depends on the history of its bureaucracies and how they have dealt with the country's minorities. This is why the same migrant group fares so differently in two places. In New Zealand, a settler state with a Treaty framework for protecting indigenous (Māori) culture, preserving Samoan culture is a fundable goal. In the United States, with its history of racial classification, difference is read along a race-and-class axis, and cultural claims fall on deaf ears.

Gershon then sketches the deep background: colonial indirect rule, under which Samoan chiefs learned to represent "Samoan custom" strategically to win resources — the birthplace of what she calls cultural expertise. She reviews the waves of migration since the 1950s, but warns against over-using them: people today move back and forth constantly, so contemporary Samoan communities in diaspora are far more varied than any "waves" scheme suggests.

Finally she names the moment she is studying: the 1990s, when neoliberal welfare reform in both countries (the US Personal Responsibility Act of 1996, New Zealand's 1989 Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act) was pushing onto families the labour governments once carried. Living in diaspora, Samoan migrants navigate multiple social orders at once — family, church, and state — and must keep deciding, context by context, what counts as cultural and what counts as acultural.
